issues: The quote is verbatim (--check FOUND on 2026-09-23, fresh fetch) on the IEEE SA standard page. It supports the step. The page's 'Published: 2026-01-20' matches the source date.

The support text says the signature scheme 'is not specified in public materials'. That is false as written. (1) The normative text of IEEE 7012-2025 (free on IEEE Xplore) deliberately leaves the method open. Cl. 5.4.2: 'Contractual agreements shall be signed electronically by both party’s agents using any standard method agreed upon for that purpose.' Cl. 5.4 has both agents sign 'on behalf of each party'. Cl. 5.2.2 requires digital copies to be delivered to both parties 'immediately upon agreement signing'. Cl. 5.4.5 lists public keys among the identifiers a named party may use. (2) The MyTerms team's individual Internet-Draft draft-curtis-myterms-01 (MCNP, 20 May 2026, no IETF standing) specifies a scheme in sec. 4. It has three levels of attestation: a server-trusted checkbox, an 'EdDSA JWT' / JWS (RFC 7515) over JCS-canonicalised JSON (RFC 8785) using a key from the signer's DID, and the same plus a zero-knowledge audit record. The step-2 verifier flagged the same point.

Nuance for the action ('each agent signs'): IEEE 7012 requires both agents to sign. In the MCNP draft, however, the site's agent must sign only if its DID is listed in the agreement ('MAY include the ENTITY AGENT's DID id, and if it is included they MUST sign'), and Level 1 'signing' is a checkbox. The action describes 7012 behaviour, so it is kept. The support text now notes the difference.

fieldFixes.supportInPublicMaterials: IEEE 7012 abstract: if both agree, the agreement is signed electronically by both parties or their agents. Cl. 5.4 has both agents sign and record the agreement 'on behalf of each party'. Cl. 5.4.2 leaves the method open ('any standard method agreed upon for that purpose'), and cl. 5.2.2 requires digital copies to be delivered to both parties immediately on signing. The MyTerms team's individual Internet-Draft (draft-curtis-myterms-01, no IETF standing) proposes a concrete scheme with three levels of attestation: a server-trusted checkbox, an EdDSA-signed JWS over canonicalised JSON using a key from the signer's decentralised identifier (DID), and the same plus a zero-knowledge audit record. In that draft the site's agent must sign only if its DID is listed in the agreement.

Sec. 4.1 (FOUND): 'When PERSON AGENTs sign agreements, there are 3 levels of attestation, one of which MUST be attested to for the agreement to be valid.' issues: All three quotes are verbatim (--check FOUND on 2026-09-23, fresh fetch). Source 2's quote ends 'Cart Mandate .' with a stray space. The page markup is 'Cart Mandate.', and the space is an extraction artefact; the on-page text 'Cart Mandate.' is NOT-FOUND by the tool because of that artefact. The quote is replaced with the next sentence, which is clean and is what actually supports 'records the price and items'.

'AP2's cart mandate' is out of date. AP2 v0.2 (released on GitHub 28 April 2026, when Google donated AP2 to the FIDO Alliance) says: 'AP2 defines two Mandate types: Checkout Mandate and Payment Mandate.' The Cart Mandate is the September 2025 v0.1 term. Corrected.

'Records the price and items but not privacy terms' is imprecise. In AP2 v0.2 the Checkout Mandate is bound by hash to a merchant-signed checkout JWT. When AP2 is used with the Universal Commerce Protocol, that payload 'MUST be the Checkout object'. The UCP Checkout object's required links array is described as 'Links to be displayed by the platform (Privacy Policy, TOS). Mandatory for legal compliance.' So the payment-side record can carry a link to the shop's OWN privacy policy. What it does not carry is the person's IEEE 7012 agreement. Reworded.

The support text says the standard leaves 'the form and storage location' open. That repeats the MyTerms FAQ but overstates. The normative text fixes the record's minimum content: cl. 5.2.4 (agreement and handshake terms, date, time stamp, pseudonymous or explicit identifiers, unique contract ID) and cl. 5.4.4 (exact time, date and location; 'Identical, immutable copies'). It leaves only the storage medium open: 'pods ... remote or cloud storage, local file folders ... Storage shall be substitutable.' The MCNP draft (sec. 4.2) also proposes a retrieval API. The step-2 verifier flagged the same point.

The support text cites 'IEEE 7012', but the record had no IEEE source. Cl. 5.4.4 of the full text is added. No mention of MyTerms or IEEE 7012 was found in the AP2 v0.2 specification, its mandate pages or the UCP checkout page. The claim that linking the two records is unspecified stands.

fieldFixes.action: ILLUSTRATIVE. Maya's agent stores its copy in her personal records; the shop stores an identical copy. The purchase itself runs under a separate payment protocol, for example AP2's checkout mandate (called the Cart Mandate when AP2 launched in September 2025). That mandate binds the items and price, and a checkout built on the Universal Commerce Protocol can also link to the shop's own privacy policy, but it carries no IEEE 7012 agreement.
fieldFixes.supportInPublicMaterials: IEEE 7012 cl. 5.2.2 and 5.4.4: signed agreements shall be identical in both parties' data stores, as 'identical, immutable copies' kept for 'possible later access, auditing, or dispute resolution'. The standard fixes the record's minimum content (terms, date, time stamp, identifiers and a unique contract ID in cl. 5.2.4; time, date and location in cl. 5.4.4) but leaves the storage medium open ('Storage shall be substitutable'). The MyTerms FAQ likewise says the record's form and storage are 'left open'. The MyTerms team's individual Internet-Draft (draft-curtis-myterms-01, no IETF standing) proposes an API for retrieving signed agreements. Neither IEEE 7012, that draft nor the AP2 specification says how to link a 7012 record to a payment mandate.

issues: The quote is verbatim (--check FOUND on 2026-09-23, fresh fetch) under the FAQ entry 'What happens if a company says "No" to my terms?'. It supports the step.

The support text understates the standard. The FAQ says the agent 'can record' a refusal, but IEEE 7012-2025 makes it mandatory. Cl. 5.2.4: 'The recorder shall record rejected agreements including date, time, and entity refusing the offer.' Cl. 5.3.1: 'If an agreement is not reached, a record shall be generated to document rejection.' Cl. 5.1 has the person's agent record the refusal 'in its own private data store'. The counterpoint verifier (agents-8) reached the same finding.

'What the agent then does is a product decision, not specified in public materials' is wrong. The standard anticipates exactly this behaviour, as should/may guidance rather than a mandate. Cl. 5.2.1.3 says the proposer 'may notify the person of refusals and ask for guidance'. It also says 'Negotiator notifications and requests should be set globally so the person can track refusals to their terms or simply not interact with anyone who refuses without notification.' Informative Annex B.1 (alternative paths b and c) says: 'Individuals may decide to set the agent to reject any app or site that does not accept terms and navigate to sites that would accept terms as substitutions.' The action's 'following her settings, shops elsewhere' is therefore directly supported.

Context, not an error: under cl. 5.3.1 a declining shop could instead have made one counter-offer (see step 4). A shop that rejects outright 'cannot bar an individual from utilizing free or public information or services', which does not apply to a paid purchase.

fieldFixes.supportInPublicMaterials: IEEE 7012 makes recording a refusal mandatory: 'The recorder shall record rejected agreements including date, time, and entity refusing the offer' (cl. 5.2.4; also cl. 5.1 and 5.3.1). The MyTerms FAQ adds that the agent 'can record that outcome' and keep track of it. What happens next is left mostly to the product, but the standard anticipates this step. The agent 'may notify the person of refusals and ask for guidance', and settings 'should be set globally' so the person can 'simply not interact with anyone who refuses' (cl. 5.2.1.3). Informative Annex B.1 describes setting the agent to reject sites that do not accept terms and go to ones that will.

issues: The quote is verbatim (--check FOUND on 2026-09-23, fresh fetch) in the abstract on the IEEE SA standard page. It supports 'retrievable, auditable or disputable'.

The support text says 'which forum hears the dispute, is not specified in public materials'. That is literally true, since no court, regulator or ADR body is named, but it leaves out what the standard does require. Cl. 5.2.4: 'The individual’s agent shall have a function for submitting to anyone including auditors an agreement in dispute' and shall allow the individual to 'share documentation with regulators and legal representatives to review existing contracts on behalf of the individual'. Cl. 5.2.5 requires an auditor function that tracks sharing with auditors and regulators. Cl. 5.4.4 keeps 'identical, immutable copies' for 'possible later access, auditing, or dispute resolution'. The action (agent retrieves the record to support a complaint to the shop or a regulator) is thus a function the standard requires, not just an illustration. The step-2 verifier flagged the same point.

'How a breach is detected' is correctly described as unspecified. No breach-detection or compliance-monitoring mechanism appears in the standard's full text or the MCNP draft; the draft's Level 3 audit record proves only that signing happened.

A caveat was missing. Cl. 5.4.3: 'There shall be only two parties to each contract.' The SD-BASE record therefore binds only the shop. If the third party got the purchase data from elsewhere in the payment chain (for example a credential provider or payment processor under AP2), the record does not cover it. Added to the support text.

fieldFixes.supportInPublicMaterials: IEEE 7012 abstract: records must be kept in a form that can be retrieved, audited or disputed. Cl. 5.4.4 requires identical, immutable copies in each party's data store 'for possible later access, auditing, or dispute resolution'. Cl. 5.2.4 requires the person's agent to have 'a function for submitting to anyone including auditors an agreement in dispute' and to let the person share documentation with regulators and legal representatives. The standard does not say how a breach is detected or which court, regulator or other body decides the dispute. The record binds only the shop, because cl. 5.4.3 allows only two parties to each contract, so it does not cover payment providers or other intermediaries.
